questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought in for tea-colored urine. Two weeks ago he had a sore throat. BP is 134/80 mm Hg and urinalysis shows red blood cells and red cell casts. Which finding is universal in nephritic syndrome?
explanations: Incorrect. Hypoalbuminemia is a feature of nephrotic syndrome from heavy proteinuria.
Incorrect. Hyperlipidemia is part of the nephrotic, not nephritic, syndrome.
Incorrect. Proteinuria in nephritic syndrome is mild to moderate (<2 g/24 h), not massive.
Correct. Hematuria is present in all cases of nephritic syndrome and reflects glomerular inflammation.
Incorrect. Oliguria occurs only in severe (RPGN) cases, not all nephritic patients.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has hematuria, edema, and BP 152/94 mm Hg. A 24-hour urine collection shows 1.2 g of protein. How does this proteinuria compare with that of nephrotic syndrome?
explanations: Incorrect. Nephritic proteinuria is lighter than the heavy nephrotic-range proteinuria.
Incorrect. >=3.5 g/24 h defines nephrotic syndrome, not nephritic.
Correct. Nephritic syndrome typically has mild to moderate proteinuria (<2 g/24 h), unlike the heavier proteinuria of nephrotic syndrome.
Incorrect. Variable proteinuria is part of the nephritic picture; it is not absent.
Incorrect. >10 g/24 h would be far in the nephrotic range.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has nephritic syndrome with rising serum creatinine. According to the brick, what is the unifying pathophysiologic mechanism across the various causative diseases?
explanations: Incorrect. Foot process effacement is a hallmark of minimal change disease, a nephrotic process.
Correct. An inflammatory glomerular immune response is common to all the disorders that produce nephritic syndrome.
Incorrect. Cast-driven tubular obstruction is not the unifying mechanism.
Incorrect. Renal artery stenosis is a vascular cause of hypertension, not nephritic syndrome.
Incorrect. Interstitial fibrosis is a chronic feature, not the inflammatory mechanism the brick highlights.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with nephritic syndrome undergoes biopsy. The pathologist describes increased mesangial, endothelial, and parietal epithelial cells with infiltrating neutrophils. Which feature is being described?
explanations: Incorrect. Membrane thickening alone (e.g., membranous nephropathy) is associated with nephrotic syndrome.
Incorrect. Podocyte effacement is a hallmark of nephrotic, not nephritic, syndrome.
Incorrect. Tubulointerstitial nephritis affects tubules and interstitium, not the glomerulus.
Incorrect. Sclerosis describes scarring, not active proliferation.
Correct. Proliferative glomerular disease is characterized by glomerular hypercellularity from mesangial, endothelial, parietal epithelial, and inflammatory cells.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with rapidly rising serum creatinine and oliguria. Renal biopsy shows proliferating parietal epithelial cells, macrophages, and fibroblasts filling Bowman space. Which finding is described?
explanations: Incorrect. Tram-tracking is seen in MPGN but does not describe the Bowman space lesion.
Incorrect. Mesangial expansion is seen in many GNs but is not the crescent described.
Incorrect. Spike-and-dome deposits describe membranous nephropathy, a nephrotic disease.
Correct. Glomerular crescents form in Bowman space from proliferating parietal epithelial cells, macrophages, and fibroblasts and are characteristic of RPGN.
Incorrect. Tubular atrophy is a chronic finding unrelated to crescent formation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman develops oliguria and a serum creatinine that doubles over a few weeks. Biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli. Which clinical syndrome does this define?
explanations: Incorrect. Acute interstitial nephritis is a tubulointerstitial process, not crescentic glomerular disease.
Correct. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is defined by rapidly falling GFR and crescents on biopsy, most often from anti-GBM disease or GPA.
Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria, not crescents.
Incorrect. Chronic kidney disease evolves over months to years, not weeks.
Incorrect. Renal artery stenosis is a vascular disorder, not crescentic GN.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has hemoptysis, dyspnea, and hematuria with red cell casts. Serum creatinine is rising rapidly. Which serologic test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
explanations: Correct. Anti-GBM antibodies confirm anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome), which causes pulmonary hemorrhage and crescentic GN.
Incorrect. ASO suggests poststreptococcal GN, which does not typically cause hemoptysis.
Incorrect. Anti-dsDNA suggests lupus nephritis.
Incorrect. p-ANCA is associated with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not anti-GBM disease.
Incorrect. Hepatitis C antibody points toward MPGN with cryoglobulinemia, not Goodpasture.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops gross hematuria 1 day after the onset of a viral upper respiratory infection. He has no rash, arthritis, or extrarenal symptoms. Which glomerular disease is most likely?
explanations: Incorrect. GPA presents with sinusitis, rash, and dyspnea in addition to renal disease.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM disease causes pulmonary hemorrhage in addition to nephritis.
Incorrect. Lupus nephritis is preceded by SLE with rash, arthritis, and serologies.
Correct. IgA nephropathy classically presents with hematuria during or shortly after a viral upper respiratory infection, with no extrarenal signs.
Incorrect. Postinfectious GN typically follows strep pharyngitis or skin infection by 1-2 weeks, not concurrent with a URI.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old girl has hematuria, mild edema, and BP 138/86 mm Hg 2 weeks after a sore throat treated with amoxicillin. C3 is low and ASO is positive. Which diagnosis is most likely?
explanations: Incorrect. IgA nephropathy follows a URI within days, not 1-2 weeks, and ASO is not the marker.
Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy is a nephrotic, not nephritic, disease.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM disease causes pulmonary hemorrhage and confirmatory anti-GBM antibodies.
Correct. Hematuria 1-2 weeks after strep pharyngitis with low C3 and a positive ASO titer is classic for poststreptococcal (postinfectious) GN.
Incorrect. GPA presents with sinusitis, purpura, and a positive c-ANCA, not a recent strep infection.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has malar rash, arthritis, hematuria with red cell casts, and 3.6 g/24 h proteinuria. Both nephritic and nephrotic features are present. Which disease most often produces this overlap?
explanations: Incorrect. IgA nephropathy can be nephritic or nephrotic but rarely both at the same time and lacks the SLE features.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM disease produces severe nephritis with hemoptysis, not nephrotic-range proteinuria.
Correct. Lupus nephritis can present simultaneously with both nephritic and nephrotic features and is suggested by the rash, arthritis, and lab profile.
Incorrect. PSGN does not typically reach nephrotic-range proteinuria.
Incorrect. GPA features sinusitis and purpura, not the lupus profile.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C develops hematuria, hypertension, and reduced GFR. Cryoglobulins are positive and serum C3 is low. Which glomerular disease is most likely?
explanations: Incorrect. Minimal change disease is a pediatric nephrotic disease.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM disease is not associated with hepatitis C or cryoglobulinemia.
Incorrect. IgA nephropathy follows a URI and is not associated with cryoglobulins or low C3.
Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy is a nephrotic disease.
Correct. Hepatitis C with cryoglobulinemia and low complement is the classic setup for membranoproliferative GN.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has sinusitis, purpuric rash, dyspnea, hematuria with red cell casts, and rising creatinine. Which serologic test is most likely positive?
explanations: Incorrect. ASO suggests poststreptococcal GN.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM disease produces hemoptysis, not sinusitis.
Incorrect. Anti-dsDNA suggests lupus nephritis, with arthritis and rash but not sinusitis.
Correct. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis presents with sinusitis, rash, and dyspnea and is associated with a positive c-ANCA.
Incorrect. Cryoglobulins are tied to hepatitis C-associated MPGN.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with a long history of asthma develops fever, abdominal pain, neuropathy, and purpura. Hematuria and red cell casts are noted, peripheral eosinophilia is present, and p-ANCA is positive. Which disease is most likely?
explanations: Incorrect. Lupus nephritis lacks asthma history and eosinophilia.
Incorrect. IgA vasculitis presents with purpura, arthralgia, and abdominal pain but not asthma or eosinophilia.
Incorrect. GPA presents with sinusitis and a positive c-ANCA, not asthma or p-ANCA.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM disease causes pulmonary hemorrhage, not asthma-like illness.
Correct. Asthma history, eosinophilia, neuropathy, and a positive p-ANCA are classic for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy has palpable purpura on the buttocks, abdominal pain, arthralgias, and hematuria. He has no antecedent strep infection. Which disease is most likely?
explanations: Correct. IgA vasculitis classically presents with purpura, arthralgias, abdominal pain, and nephritis in children.
Incorrect. Postinfectious GN follows a strep infection by 1-2 weeks and lacks the purpura/arthralgia syndrome.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM disease causes hemoptysis and is rare in children.
Incorrect. Lupus nephritis is uncommon in young boys and has different serologies.
Incorrect. GPA produces sinusitis and dyspnea, not the IgA vasculitis triad.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with nephritic syndrome has urine microscopy showing red blood cells. Which urinary finding is highly specific for glomerular disease?
explanations: Incorrect. Hyaline casts are nonspecific and seen in many conditions, including normal concentrated urine.
Incorrect. Waxy casts indicate chronic kidney disease, not specifically glomerular disease.
Correct. Red blood cell casts are highly specific for glomerular disease and strongly suggest nephritic syndrome.
Incorrect. Crystalluria reflects stone disease or metabolic disorders, not glomerular injury.
Incorrect. Pyuria suggests urinary tract infection or interstitial nephritis.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has hematuria. Urine microscopy shows abnormally shaped red blood cells with surface blebs and irregular contours. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
explanations: Incorrect. Serum hemolysis is unrelated to urine RBC morphology.
Incorrect. Lower tract bleeding (e.g., stones, tumors) typically yields isomorphic RBCs.
Incorrect. Contamination would not produce a uniform dysmorphic pattern.
Correct. Dysmorphic RBCs are suggestive of glomerular disease and nephritic syndrome.
Incorrect. Dysmorphic RBCs are pathologic, not normal.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with suspected nephritic syndrome has serum complement measured. Which combination of complement findings is characteristic of lupus nephritis?
explanations: Incorrect. Normal complements would not fit the brick's described pattern for lupus nephritis.
Incorrect. Both elevated complements would not suggest active glomerular consumption.
Incorrect. Low C3 alone with normal C4 is more typical of postinfectious GN or MPGN.
Incorrect. High C3 with low C4 is not the lupus pattern in this brick.
Correct. Lupus nephritis classically shows low C3 and low C4, distinguishing it from PSGN and MPGN, in which only C3 is low.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has nephritic syndrome and a low C3. Which set of diagnoses should be considered based on this finding alone?
explanations: Correct. Postinfectious GN, lupus nephritis, and membranoproliferative GN all classically present with low C3.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM disease and IgA nephropathy do not typically lower complement.
Incorrect. Minimal change disease and FSGS are nephrotic and do not lower complement.
Incorrect. GPA and anti-GBM disease are pauci-immune or anti-GBM-mediated and do not consume C3.
Incorrect. IgA-mediated diseases do not typically lower complement.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman has nephritic syndrome and rapidly rising serum creatinine over a few weeks. According to the brick, when is renal biopsy always indicated?
explanations: Incorrect. Stable mild hematuria with normal renal function may be observed without immediate biopsy.
Incorrect. Suspected PSGN is usually managed supportively without biopsy.
Correct. Biopsy is always needed in RPGN because early treatment of causes like anti-GBM disease and GPA is critical to preserving kidney function.
Incorrect. Asymptomatic microscopic hematuria does not by itself mandate biopsy.
Incorrect. Isolated low-grade proteinuria is not the brick's indication for required biopsy.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy has hematuria, low C3, and a positive ASO titer 2 weeks after strep pharyngitis. Renal function is normal. Which best describes the management?
explanations: Incorrect. Plasmapheresis is reserved for anti-GBM disease.
Incorrect. Cyclophosphamide is used for severe lupus nephritis or GPA, not PSGN.
Correct. PSGN is managed supportively with fluid restriction, diuretics for edema, and BP control; most patients recover spontaneously.
Incorrect. PSGN typically does not require biopsy because the diagnosis is clinically obvious and treatment would not change.
Incorrect. Long-term prednisone is not standard for PSGN.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with biopsy-proven anti-GBM disease has rising creatinine and pulmonary hemorrhage. Beyond immunosuppression, which therapy is specifically indicated?
explanations: Incorrect. Antibiotics have no role in this autoimmune disease.
Incorrect. Hemodialysis is supportive for renal failure but does not treat the antibody-mediated disease.
Incorrect. An ACE inhibitor alone does not address the immunologic injury in anti-GBM disease.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics treat volume overload but not the underlying disease.
Correct. Anti-GBM disease requires plasmapheresis to remove the damaging circulating antibodies.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with biopsy-proven lupus nephritis is started on disease-modifying therapy. Which class of drugs is the mainstay for this and other inflammatory glomerular diseases?
explanations: Incorrect. Beta-blockers do not treat the underlying glomerular inflammation.
Incorrect. Statins manage hyperlipidemia, not the immunologic injury.
Correct. Immunosuppressive drugs such as prednisone and cyclophosphamide are the mainstay for inflammatory glomerular diseases like lupus nephritis and GPA.
Incorrect. Calcium channel blockers lower blood pressure but do not modify glomerular disease.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics are supportive for edema, not curative.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with chronic glomerular disease has BP 144/92 mm Hg and 1.8 g/24 h proteinuria. Which medication class is preferred to lower BP, reduce proteinuria, and slow progression?
explanations: Correct. ACE inhibitors or ARBs lower BP, reduce proteinuria, and slow progression of chronic glomerular disease by reducing intraglomerular pressure.
Incorrect. Thiazides lower BP but do not specifically reduce proteinuria or slow glomerular progression.
Incorrect. Beta-blockers do not have the same antiproteinuric effect.
Incorrect. Calcium channel blockers lower BP but do not preferentially reduce proteinuria.
Incorrect. Alpha-blockers are not first-line for nephritic patients with proteinuria.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with nephritic syndrome from GPA develops a GFR of 8 mL/min, confusion, and serum K+ of 6.4 mEq/L. According to the brick, which intervention is now needed?
explanations: Incorrect. Stopping immunosuppression would worsen the underlying disease.
Incorrect. ACE inhibitors can worsen hyperkalemia and reduce GFR further in this setting.
Incorrect. The diagnosis is already known; biopsy will not address the acute uremia.
Incorrect. Cryoprecipitate has no role in uremia management.
Correct. Dialysis is indicated when GFR falls to very low levels and uremic signs, hyperkalemia, or acidosis occur.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with hematuria has C3 measured as part of his work-up. According to the brick, which group of nephritic diseases is associated with a low C3?
explanations: Incorrect. IgA nephropathy and Alport syndrome do not typically lower C3.
Correct. Postinfectious GN, lupus nephritis, and membranoproliferative GN are the classic low-C3 nephritic diseases in the brick.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM disease and GPA do not consume complement; they are antibody- or pauci-immune-mediated.
Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy and FSGS are nephrotic diseases without C3 consumption.
Incorrect. Minimal change disease and Alport syndrome are not associated with low C3.
